text.p: A telephone that can surf the Internet as well as make calls was unveiled Friday by a telephone maker and a Silicon Valley start-up.

The "iPhone" developed by start-up InfoGear Technology Corp. and telephone maker Cidco Inc. can be used to send and receive electronic mail, visit the World Wide Web and conduct some Web transactions, Infogear said.
The phone features a screen that measures 7.4 inches diagonally and a pop-out keyboard for tasks like writing e-mail or typing in Web page addresses.

"This product is not designed to replace the PC but to get on and off the Web quickly and allow consumers cheap, easy access," InfoGear President Robert Marshall said in an interview a day before Friday's unveiling in Las Vegas.

"You can use it to order flowers, make travel arrangements, check stock quotes -- you know, on the way out the door you want to do something but don't want to spend three minutes booting up the PC," he added.
The phone, however, will face a lot of competition by the time it hits the retail market, which is expected by June.

Marshall said he expected the phone to sell for about $500. However, Morgan Hill, Calif.-based Cidco and InfoGear of Redwood City, Calif., plan to sell it initially to telephone carriers to market to their subscribers.

Sprint Corp. will soon start a pilot programme selling the phone in a package with its Internet service, and InfoGear said Medical Telecommunications Associates Inc. has agreed to market the phones to its medical information customers.

Cidco and InfoGear also announced that several companies would make products that work with the iPhone, including VeriFone Inc., which is making a card-swipe secure payment system to attach to the device, and BigBook Inc., which will adopt a version of its online yellow pages software for the phone.

The iPhone technology was developed by InfoGear and was based on work started at National Semiconductor Corp., Marshall said. The device uses National Semiconductor chips. Cidco, which makes advanced telephones and caller ID systems, developed the telephone hardware.
However, the phone will not be the only alternative to the personal computer for accessing the Net.

The idea of making easy Internet access available via simple appliances and phones has become almost a calling for electronics manufacturers. Since Oracle Corp. released its "network computer" software for low-cost, network-only computing, several companies have said they are developing Internet phones using the software.

Acknowledging that other Net phones are in the market or in development, Marshall said the iPhone can display graphics -- and thus pages from the Web -- while most of the competing products are text-only.
